en: Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The Twenty Verses on Consciousness-Only (Viṃśatikākārikā): This [world] is indeed consciousness-only, because there is the appearance of non-existent objects, just as a person with cataracts sees non-existent hairs, moons, and so forth. (Vk 1)
If representation were without an object, then the restriction of place and time,
the lack of restriction regarding the mental continuum, and the performance of purposeful action would not be possible.
The restriction of place and so forth is established as in a dream;
furthermore, the lack of restriction regarding the mental continuum is established by all [who see] the river of pus and so on. (Vk 3)

The performance of purposeful action is like [the effects of] a dream; furthermore, everything regarding the vision of hell-wardens and so forth, as well as the suffering inflicted by them, is like [the experience of] hell.
The birth of animals occurs in heaven just as it does not in hell;
nor does it occur for pretas, because they do not experience the suffering born of that [birth].
If it is accepted that, through those karmas, there is likewise the arising and transformation of the elements (*bhūta*) therein, why is this not also accepted for consciousness (*vijñāna*)?
The latent impression of an action is conceived as being in one place, while its fruit is conceived as being in another;
why indeed is it not accepted as being in the very same place where the impression resides?
The existence of the sense-bases such as form was taught with a specific intention toward those people who were to be converted, just like [the teaching on] spontaneously born beings.
From whatever own-seed a representation arises having a certain appearance,
the Sage spoke of those two as its twofold sense-field.

For in this way there is entry into the selflessness of the person; however, otherwise, the teaching [of emptiness] is for the purpose of entering into the selflessness of phenomena by means of the imagined nature.
That object is neither one nor many when analyzed into atoms;
nor are they [the atoms] combined, because the atom itself is not established.
Through simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms], the atom would have six parts;
because the six occupy the same location, the entire mass would be no larger than a single atom.
If there is no conjunction of atoms, then in their aggregate, whose would that [conjunction] be?
Nor is it the case that their conjunction is not established because of their lack of parts. (13)
For that which possesses a distinction of spatial directions, unity is not tenable.
Or else, how could there be shadow and obstruction? If it is argued that these do not belong to a composite whole, they cannot belong to the atom either.
If [the mind] were a single entity, there would be no sequential occurrence; nor could there be simultaneous grasping and non-grasping;
nor would there be the existence of multiple distinct occurrences, nor the non-perception of subtle objects.
Just as there is a cognition of direct perception in dreams and the like, at that time the object is not seen; how then can its status as a direct perception be maintained?
It has been stated how representation appears as that [object], and from that, memory arises;
one who has not awakened does not realize the absence of the objects seen in a dream. (17)
The restriction of representation occurs mutually through mutual predominance;
because the mind is impaired by torpor in a dream, its result is not the same [as that of waking].
Death is a transformation resulting from a specific representation of another, just as the loss of memory and other such states occur in others through the power of the minds of piśācas and the like.
Or how was the Daṇḍaka forest emptied by the wrath of the sages? Or how is it established by that [example] that the punishment of the mind is a great offense?
How is the knowledge of those who know the minds of others not in accordance with reality? It is like the knowledge of one's own mind due to ignorance, or like the sphere of experience of a Buddha.
This Proof of Representation-Only has been composed by me according to my own ability;
however, it is in every respect inconceivable, for it is the domain of the Buddhas.
The Twenty Verses are completed.
